newsitem.title: USA: Administration aims to save $1 billion in energy costs.
newsitem.headline: Administration aims to save $1 billion in energy costs.

text.p: The U.S. Energy Department Wednesday announced a new programme that aims to save the federal government $1 billion a year in energy costs for federal buildings across the country.

In the first step of the programme, Energy Secretary Federico Pena awarded contracts that will be worth a total of up to $750 million to five sets of companies to upgrade energy systems in federal facilities in eight Western states.
Energy Department officials said when the five contracts were fully carried out they would save the government as much as $1.5 billion in energy costs over about five years.

The companies that won the contracts were: Energy Pacific, a joint venture of Enova Corp. and Pacific Enterprises; Honeywell Inc.; Johnson Controls Inc.; ERI Services Inc; and a joint venture of the Bentley Co./BMP Team, Puget Sound Energy, and MacDonald Miller Co.
In addition, the department plans to make six more similar awards over the next two years for a total contract value of about $5 billion.
"The federal government spends $4 billion a year to power our buildings," Pena said at a news briefing. "It makes the U.S. government the single largest energy consumer in the United States."
President Clinton said the government should aim to cut energy use by 30 percent in the 500,000 federal buildings around the United States by 2005.
The government will pay the companies no money up front but will finance the energy efficiency upgrades by paying the companies half of the savings in its future electric bills.

Once the investments under all of the contracts are made to retrofit federal buildings, the improvements are expected to eliminate the equivalent of the amount of pollution produced in one year by about nine coal-fired power plants and meet Clinton's energy savings goal.

Company officials said that the energy savings could be achieved by improving heating and cooling systems, lighting, and insulation at the federal buildings, or could involve changing the fuel used at those buildings.

The U.S. Coast Guard, the Federal Aviation Administration and the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration have already lined up to place orders under the new contracts for facilities in Alaska and Washington State.
